relations.note: A colonial genealogical tradition describes Chalchiuhtlicue as Tlaloc’s wife or consort.
They jointly receive offerings, impersonation, and sacrifice in the water-deity ceremonial cycle.

relations.myth: Proposal of their son for solar office
relations.note: The couple have a son whom Tlaloc proposes should become the sun.
Sahagún’s informants explicitly identify Chalchiuhtlicue as sister of the rain gods.
Chalchiuhtlicue and the Tlaloque share rites, offerings, impersonation, and sacrificial ceremonies.

relations.myth: Council over whose son becomes the sun
relations.note: Chalchiuhtlicue participates with Quetzalcoatl in a divine dispute over the solar candidate.
Both belong to the collective divine recipients of the opening rainmaking festival.
After washing through Chalchiuhtlicue’s water, the infant is lifted and presented to Tonatiuh.
Citlalatonac is invoked after Chalchiuhtlicue’s washing when the infant is raised toward celestial powers.
Citlalicue is invoked after Chalchiuhtlicue’s washing when the infant is raised toward celestial powers.

relations.myth: Fourth presentation of the washed infant
relations.note: Tlaltecuhtli receives the fourth presentation after Chalchiuhtlicue’s water has washed the infant.
Ometecuhtli sends or generates the child whom Chalchiuhtlicue’s water receives and cleanses.
Omecihuatl sends or generates the child whom Chalchiuhtlicue’s water receives and cleanses.
Sahagún calls Chalchiuhtlicue another Juno as a comparison for European readers.
